summary:
Chelyabinsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out as the conditions in force across every region of the country. Same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Public expression carries criminal exposure. 'Gay propaganda' offences bring fines of up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and a repeat offence can be prosecuted criminally with a sentence of up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

The Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and people in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and records that at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between December 2022 and March 2024. The note contains no region-specific findings for Chelyabinsk Oblast; the national conditions it documents apply to this oblast.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume is documented by Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts issued 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays are punishable under the criminal code by up to four years in prison.

On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years. The charge shows that commercial and cultural activity, not only visible protest, attracts extremism proceedings.

For anyone leaving the country rather than entering it, the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chelyabinsk Oblast have no statutory protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment, and same-sex marriage is not available. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been prohibited since 2023, so a resident's documents and medical care cannot be brought into line with their gender identity through any domestic route.

Ordinary conduct carries administrative risk for residents as well as visitors. Displaying symbols of the banned organisation is prosecuted as an administrative offence with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and a second display moves the matter into the criminal code with up to four years. Participation in the designated movement carries two to six years and organising carries six to ten years.

The Home Office assessment that trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates face treatment amounting to persecution applies to residents seeking protection abroad, and at least 139 people were affected by anti-LGBT+ enforcement nationwide between December 2022 and March 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports enforcement actions, raids, arrests or court proceedings specific to Chelyabinsk Oblast. The oblast-level picture is unresolved: whether the extremism designation has been applied by courts in Chelyabinsk, and how often, is not sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether Chelyabinsk Oblast has any regional measures on document amendment, facilities access or healthcare provision beyond the federal bans; that is unresolved rather than confirmed as absent.

The UK Home Office note sets national conditions and explicitly contains no region-specific findings, so any oblast-level variation in practice would have to be sourced separately.
